quiz.scale: -2 = strongly disagree, -1 = disagree, 0 = neutral/mixed, +1 = agree, +2 = strongly agree; null = the party has no public position we could find (never guessed). Positions are the party's, relative to the statement text.

scoring.method: For each statement both the user and the party answered: agreement = 1 - |user - party| / 4. Weighted average over those statements using user importance weights (default 1; suggest 0.5/1/2). Report coverage = statements the party has a position on, out of statements the user answered; flag matches with coverage below 10 statements, and blend toward 0.5 (neutral) by adjusted = (sum_w*agree + k*0.5) / (sum_w + k) with k = 3 so thin records are not over-rewarded.

statements.text: New Zealand should introduce a capital gains tax (for example on investment and commercial property).
statements.explainer: New Zealand has no general capital gains tax; Labour is campaigning on a 28% tax on gains from investment and commercial property (family homes, farms, shares and KiwiSaver excluded).

national.evidence: "No new taxes, including no capital gains tax."

labour.evidence: Create a 28% capital gains tax on commercial and residential property, excluding the family home, from 1 July 2027.

green.evidence: Prefers wider wealth taxes; Green MP Teanau Tuiono called Labour's CGT "quite narrow" and said the Greens' wealth tax would be more effective. Greens also propose a 33% capital acquisitions (inheritance/gift) tax.

act.evidence: KPMG 2026 tax tracker lists ACT: "No capital gains tax" (plus a crypto capital-gains exemption).

alliance.evidence: "The Alliance will introduce a broad-based capital gains tax, covering investment property, shares..." (33%, excluding the family home).

statements.text: There should be an annual wealth tax on people with very large fortunes (for example net wealth over $2–10 million).
statements.explainer: Greens propose 2.5% on net wealth over $10m; Te Pāti Māori a tiered tax from $2m; Labour has ruled a wealth tax out.

national.evidence: National's Economic Plan lists the Greens/Te Pāti Māori "Asset Tax" among "nine new taxes" it opposes; promises "no new taxes".

labour.evidence: KPMG tracker: "Chris Hipkins has ruled out a wealth/inheritance tax."

green.evidence: Introduce a 2.5% tax on net wealth over $10 million (family homes exempt).

act.evidence: KPMG tracker lists ACT: "No wealth tax/inheritance tax."

nz-first.evidence: KPMG tracker: NZ First position "Not stated, has previously opposed such taxes."

te-pati-maori.evidence: Implement a targeted wealth tax: 1.5% on net assets $2–5m, 2% on $5–10m, 2.5% over $10m ("A Kiwi Tax Plan").

alliance.evidence: "2.5% Wealth Tax: An annual tax on individual net wealth above $2 million."

statements.text: GST should be removed from food such as fresh fruit and vegetables.
statements.explainer: GST is charged at 15% on almost all food. Removing it from some food was debated in 2023; in 2026 Te Pāti Māori offers a "No GST on Kai" credit instead.

te-pati-maori.evidence: "Remove GST costs from kai" — delivered as an income-tax "Kai Credit" worth about eight weeks of groceries for people earning under $60,000, rather than a GST exemption at the till.

animal-justice.evidence: "Remove GST from fruits, vegetables, legumes, nuts and other core plant-based foods."

conservative.evidence: Favours a lower overall GST rate (12.5%) rather than food exemptions: "A lower rate of GST -12.5% is favoured."

statements.text: The first slice of everyone's income (e.g. the first $10,000 or more) should be tax-free.
statements.explainer: NZ taxes income from the first dollar (10.5% up to $15,600). Several parties propose a tax-free threshold paid for by other taxes.

green.evidence: Make the first $10,000 people earn tax-free.

nz-first.evidence: KPMG tracker: NZ First would "make the lowest tax bracket (currently $14,000 pa) of income tax-free no later than 1 April 2027."

te-pati-maori.evidence: Make the first $30,000 earned tax-free.

alliance.evidence: "Make the first $20,000 of every person's income completely tax-free."

vision-nz.evidence: "Make the first $25,000 of personal income completely tax-free."

statements.text: The government should force the big supermarket chains to be broken up or restructured to increase competition.
statements.explainer: Two groups (Foodstuffs and Woolworths) dominate groceries. Proposals range from splitting Foodstuffs to a state-owned supermarket, versus easing entry for new competitors.

national.evidence: Separate the Foodstuffs business into two nationwide cooperatives (a targeted restructure rather than a full break-up).

labour.evidence: Separate wholesale food businesses from the retail supermarket sector.

green.evidence: Break up the supermarket duopoly and use part of it to create a government-owned supermarket.

act.evidence: "While other parties destroy investor confidence by proposing break-ups, price controls, or state-run alternatives, ACT will focus on the barriers that make it hard for new competitors to enter."

nz-first.evidence: Separate the Foodstuffs supermarket chain into two national cooperatives and give the Grocery Commissioner more powers.

opportunity.evidence: Give the Commerce Commission greater powers and more market support to small businesses (no specific break-up).

statements.text: The minimum wage should rise every year by at least the rate of inflation.
statements.explainer: Minimum-wage rises since 2023 have been below inflation. ACT proposes a three-year freeze.

labour.evidence: Increase the minimum wage every year; answered "Yes" to NZCTU: set the minimum wage above inflation for the next 3 years.

green.evidence: NZCTU scorecard: "Yes" to setting the minimum wage above inflation for the next three years.

act.evidence: Freeze the minimum wage for three years.

nz-first.evidence: Increase the minimum wage in line with inflation; answered "Yes" to the NZCTU scorecard question.

te-pati-maori.evidence: NZCTU scorecard: "Yes" to setting the minimum wage above inflation for the next three years.

alliance.evidence: NZCTU scorecard: "Yes" to setting the minimum wage above inflation for the next three years.

womens-rights.evidence: "Minimum wages and benefits need to be increased so that all people have living incomes."

vision-nz.evidence: "Legislate the transition from the minimum wage to an annually adjusted Living Wage to protect working families from inflation."

statements.text: Fair Pay Agreements (industry-wide minimum pay and conditions negotiated by unions and employers) should be brought back.
statements.explainer: Labour introduced Fair Pay Agreements in 2022; the National-led government repealed them in December 2023.

national.evidence: Repealed the Fair Pay Agreements Act in December 2023 (all National MPs voted for repeal); NZCTU scorecard "No".

labour.evidence: NZCTU scorecard: "Yes" to restoring Fair Pay Agreements in the first 100 days.

green.evidence: Reverse changes to pay equity and fair pay agreements; NZCTU scorecard "Yes".

act.evidence: Supported the 2023 repeal; NZCTU scorecard "No".

nz-first.evidence: NZCTU scorecard: "No" to restoring Fair Pay Agreements.

te-pati-maori.evidence: NZCTU scorecard: "Yes" to restoring Fair Pay Agreements in the first 100 days.

opportunity.evidence: NZCTU scorecard: "No" to restoring Fair Pay Agreements in the first 100 days.

alliance.evidence: NZCTU scorecard: "Yes" to restoring Fair Pay Agreements in the first 100 days.

womens-rights.evidence: Advocates "reinstatement of legislative support for Fair Pay Agreements."

statements.text: Annual rent increases should be capped by law.
statements.explainer: There is currently no cap on how much rent can rise (only one increase per 12 months). The Greens propose a 2% annual cap.

national.evidence: Focuses on building more homes "rather than controlling rents" (Salient 2026 guide); points to rent increases at a 25-year low.

labour.evidence: In 2023 Chris Hipkins ruled out the Greens' rent cap, saying it was not under consideration "and would not be in the future"; Labour's 2026 rent pledge covers only state/social housing tenants.

green.evidence: Limit annual rent increases to 2 percent.

act.evidence: Favours increasing supply through deregulation and property rights "rather than measures such as rent controls" (Salient 2026 guide).

alliance.evidence: Caps social-housing rent at 25% of income (state-owned housing only).

statements.text: The government should build a lot more state and public housing.
statements.explainer: Kāinga Ora's building programme was scaled back after 2023; the government has focused on community housing providers and private supply.

national.evidence: "Focused primarily on building more homes rather than controlling rents... free up land, streamline planning and consenting" — supply-led, not a state building programme (Salient guide).

labour.evidence: Add at least 6,000 more social housing places over the next four years.

green.evidence: Increase public housing supply and housing support.

act.evidence: Favours "increasing supply through deregulation, stronger property rights and easier consenting" and "greater faith in private investment... than in direct government provision".

te-pati-maori.evidence: Increase the supply of housing in both the public and private sector; wants more public and affordable housing.

alliance.evidence: "A five-year housing plan: a massive public building programme led by Kāinga Ora, alongside a newly established Ministry of Works."

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: Mana Taumaru local build policy: hemp-panel homes built by local trainees on papakāinga, allocated to families in overcrowded or substandard housing.

statements.text: Councils should have to allow more and denser housing, such as townhouses and apartments, in our cities.
statements.explainer: Zoning rules decide how many homes can be built. Recent reforms (MDRS, "Going for Housing Growth") push councils to allow more density.

national.evidence: Wants to "free up land, streamline planning and consenting, and finance the infrastructure needed for development" (Salient guide); removing the ban on minimum car-parking is the only partial exception.

green.evidence: Encourage mixed-use areas and walkability in new housing developments.

act.evidence: Favours increasing supply through deregulation and easier consenting (Salient guide).

opportunity.evidence: Revamp zoning to reduce house prices.

statements.text: Some GP visits each year should be free for everyone.
statements.explainer: Most adults pay $20–$80+ per GP visit. Labour proposes a "Medicard" with three free visits a year, funded by its capital gains tax.

national.evidence: Says Labour's "free" promises (including the Medicard) total $18 billion and would need "nine new taxes"; offers rural doctor funding and pharmacist access instead.

labour.evidence: Make up to three GP visits a year free with a Medicard.

green.evidence: Increase free public health services.

alliance.evidence: "Elimination of costs for GP visits, dental, optical, and audiology services."

statements.text: The $5 prescription charge should be scrapped.
statements.explainer: The previous government removed the $5 prescription co-payment in 2023; the current government reinstated it for most adults in 2024.

national.evidence: Keeps the $5 charge it reinstated in 2024 for most adults, with "targeted free prescriptions to seniors" instead of universal free prescriptions.

labour.evidence: Remove the $5 charge for prescriptions (restore universal free prescriptions).

statements.text: Free school lunches should be expanded and made more generous, even if it costs more.
statements.explainer: Ka Ora, Ka Ako school lunches were kept but cut to roughly $3 a meal in 2024 under a model designed by ACT's David Seymour.

labour.evidence: Pay for school lunches that cost $5 per meal and ensure schools provide locally made lunches.

green.evidence: Keep and expand the free school lunches programme.

opportunity.evidence: Rebuild the school lunch programme.

statements.text: Charter (partnership) schools should be allowed to continue.
statements.explainer: Charter schools are state-funded but privately run. They were reintroduced in 2025 by the National-ACT-NZ First government.

labour.evidence: Labour vowed in 2024 to "get rid of" charter schools if returned to government.

green.evidence: Green alternative Budget 2025 includes "Abolition of Charter Schools Agency".

act.evidence: ACT campaigns on expanding charter schools.

statements.text: University and polytechnic study should be fees-free.
statements.explainer: Fees-free first-year study (2018) was replaced in 2025 by a smaller final-year scheme.

national.evidence: National's student policy is lowering the student-loan repayment rate to 10%, not fees-free study.

labour.evidence: Labour's 2026 student offer is a 10% student-loan cut for graduates who did not get Fees Free, not a return to fees-free study.

green.evidence: Introduce fees-free tertiary education, universal student allowances and paid placements.

alliance.evidence: Platform promises "free education and healthcare" (RNZ summary of the Alliance).

statements.text: Repeat serious offenders should face mandatory longer sentences under a "three strikes" law.
statements.explainer: Labour repealed three strikes in 2022; the current government reinstated a version in December 2024.

national.evidence: Voted for the Sentencing (Reinstating Three Strikes) Amendment Act 2024 at every reading.

labour.evidence: Voted against reinstatement; justice spokesperson Duncan Webb said three-strikes regimes did little to reduce serious crime.

green.evidence: Voted against; Tamatha Paul said it would disproportionately target Māori and increase incarceration.

act.evidence: Voted for reinstating three strikes; 2026 policy adds a minimum three-year sentence for a third burglary conviction.

nz-first.evidence: Voted for the Reinstating Three Strikes Amendment Act 2024.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Voted against the Reinstating Three Strikes Bill.

alliance.evidence: Justice policy reframes it as "Three strikes and into treatment" — prevention and rehabilitation rather than longer sentences.

conservative.evidence: Wants "meaningful consequences for serious and repeat offending" and longer sentences for repeat child sex offenders.

statements.text: We should send fewer people to prison and put more into rehabilitation and community alternatives.
statements.explainer: NZ has one of the higher imprisonment rates in the OECD, and the prison population has been rising.

national.evidence: Add 240 beds to Christchurch Men's Prison; backs tougher sentencing (three strikes).

green.evidence: Prioritise rehabilitation for convicted offenders; reduce restrictions on judges' decisions.

act.evidence: Tougher sentencing, including a mandatory minimum for a third burglary conviction.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Abolish prisons by 2040 and move towards restorative justice.

opportunity.evidence: Boost court and rehabilitation funding to reduce reoffending.

legalise-cannabis.evidence: "Education not incarceration" — redirect money from prohibition enforcement to health and education.

alliance.evidence: "Three strikes and into treatment. Prevent harm, rehabilitate, support victims."

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: "Prison Sinking Lid Policy" — shift non-violent offenders with addiction and mental-health needs out of prison into localised rehabilitation.

statements.text: Farmers should pay for their greenhouse gas emissions, for example by bringing agriculture into the Emissions Trading Scheme.
statements.explainer: Agriculture produces about half of NZ's emissions but is not priced. The government dropped plans to price farm emissions before 2030.

national.evidence: Maintain the current position of agricultural emissions not being priced or offset through the ETS.

labour.evidence: Made no commitment to price farm emissions: "in government Labour will urgently review the ETS" (Greenpeace survey answer).

green.evidence: "We will bring agricultural emissions into the ETS" (answer to Greenpeace 2026 survey).

act.evidence: Ensure agriculture is not part of the emissions trading scheme.

nz-first.evidence: "No, NZ First does not support emissions pricing in any form unless adopted by key trading partners" (Greenpeace survey).

te-pati-maori.evidence: Answered "Yes" to bringing agriculture into the ETS by mid-2027 (Greenpeace 2026 survey).

opportunity.evidence: Strengthen the ETS and include agriculture; told Greenpeace it "will explore a cap-and-trade market or novel levy structure" for biogenic methane.

animal-justice.evidence: Wants to "redirect funds away from animal agriculture, through taxes" and transition farmers to plant-based agriculture.

alliance.evidence: Replace the ETS with a carbon tax on a polluter-pays principle (no specific farm carve-out stated).

conservative.evidence: "There is no climate emergency... Laws/agreements like the Paris Accord, Zero Carbon Act, and Emissions Trading Scheme impose significant costs."

statements.text: New Zealand should keep its legal net-zero 2050 target and stay in the Paris Agreement.
statements.explainer: The Zero Carbon Act (2019, passed almost unanimously) sets a net-zero target for 2050; NZ is a party to the 2015 Paris Agreement.

labour.evidence: "Labour is fully committed to the Paris Agreement and will put New Zealand on course to meet its targets."

green.evidence: Enforce timely implementation of climate legislation and increase Zero Carbon Act reporting and transparency.

act.evidence: Repeal the Zero Carbon Act and NZ's net-zero goal.

nz-first.evidence: Says it would withdraw New Zealand from the Paris Agreement (Salient guide; KPMG tracker: "Campaigned to leave the Paris Accord").

opportunity.evidence: Retain the Climate Change Commission and ensure NZ's emissions goals align with the Paris Agreement.

nz-loyal.evidence: "End climate accords based on faulty science" (party website as quoted by RNZ).

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: "Let's get out of Paris accord and work for solutions to mitigate weather risks."

conservative.evidence: "New Zealand should leave the Paris Agreement"; all climate legislation "should be repealed or withdrawn".

vision-nz.evidence: "Restore absolute national sovereignty by leaving the United Nations and the Paris Accord."

statements.text: Ministers should be able to fast-track big infrastructure, mining and development projects past the normal consent process.
statements.explainer: The Fast-track Approvals Act 2024 lets listed projects skip the usual Resource Management Act process, with expert panels making the decisions.

national.evidence: Passed the Fast-track Approvals Act 2024 (supported at every reading) and proposes a fast-track policy statement for mining.

labour.evidence: Voted against the Act; "Labour will fix the Fast-track Approvals Act so that environmental protections are not overridden, there is public participation" (keeps a fast-track, but changed).

green.evidence: Repeal the Fast-track Approvals Act.

act.evidence: Supported the Fast-track Approvals Act at every reading.

nz-first.evidence: The Act was part of NZ First's coalition agreement; supported at every reading.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Voted against the Fast-track Approvals Act at all three readings.

opportunity.evidence: Answered "Yes" to restoring strong environmental protections and public participation in all resource consenting (Greenpeace survey).

alliance.evidence: Criticises the government for "fast-tracking legislation and using urgency for policies that harm Aotearoa New Zealand".

statements.text: Seabed mining should be banned in New Zealand waters.
statements.explainer: Trans-Tasman Resources' South Taranaki iron-sands project has applied through fast-track; several parties want a permanent ban.

national.evidence: Voted against members' bills to ban seabed mining (2023) and created the fast-track pathway used by seabed miners (Greenpeace assessment).

labour.evidence: Answered "Yes" to banning seabed mining (Greenpeace 2026 survey).

green.evidence: Answered "Yes" to banning seabed mining (Greenpeace 2026 survey).

act.evidence: Voted against seabed-mining ban bills (2023); vocal pro-mining stance (Greenpeace assessment).

nz-first.evidence: "No, NZ First does not support a ban; instead, we advocate for higher government levies on minerals extracted from coastal seabed iron sands."

te-pati-maori.evidence: Ban seabed mining.

opportunity.evidence: Permanently ban seabed mining in NZ waters.

animal-justice.evidence: Key objective: "Restrict seabed mining" (restriction rather than outright ban).

statements.text: The ban on new offshore oil and gas exploration should be brought back.
statements.explainer: Labour banned new offshore oil and gas permits in 2018; the Crown Minerals Amendment Act 2025 reversed the ban.

national.evidence: Voted to repeal the ban (Crown Minerals Amendment Act 2025).

labour.evidence: Answered "Yes" to bringing back the ban (Greenpeace survey); Hipkins has said Labour would reinstate it while honouring existing permits.

green.evidence: "Yes. The Green Party wants to see new fossil fuel extraction ended in Aotearoa."

act.evidence: Voted to repeal the ban (Crown Minerals Amendment Act 2025).

nz-first.evidence: "No. NZ First does not support reinstating a blanket ban on oil and gas exploration."

te-pati-maori.evidence: Answered "Yes" to reinstating the ban (Greenpeace survey).

opportunity.evidence: Would "not oppose a reinstatement" but considers it "probably unnecessary" and would not progress it itself.

nz-loyal.evidence: "Establish energy independence, including oil and gas" (party website as quoted by RNZ).

animal-justice.evidence: "Reverse the lifting of the offshore exploration ban and reinstate the moratorium on new fossil fuel permits."

conservative.evidence: "Actively encourage commercial oil and gas exploration."

statements.text: The government should take a bigger direct role in electricity, such as a new state-owned power company or splitting up the big power companies.
statements.explainer: Four "gentailers" (Meridian, Mercury, Genesis, Contact) both generate and retail most power. A 2025 government review rejected structural separation.

national.evidence: The National-led government's 2025 electricity review response did not include structural separation; Nicola Willis argued splitting the gentailers risked "massive instability".

green.evidence: Establish a publicly owned Crown entity ("Kiwipower") to invest in renewable generation.

act.evidence: Open power transmission to private investment; opposes break-ups and state-run alternatives.

nz-first.evidence: Divide the "generation" and "retail" arms of power companies.

opportunity.evidence: Restructure the electricity market to bring prices down; use the Crown's gentailer stakes to fund renewables.

alliance.evidence: "100 percent public ownership of electricity generation, transmission, distribution, and retail."

statements.text: Parliament should define the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi in law, as ACT's Treaty Principles Bill proposed.
statements.explainer: The Treaty Principles Bill was voted down 112–11 at its second reading in April 2025; only ACT voted for it.

national.evidence: Voted against the Bill at its second reading after supporting it only to select committee; Luxon pledged to refuse a Treaty referendum.

labour.evidence: Voted against at both readings; said the Bill's principles "did not match the principles of the Treaty".

green.evidence: Voted against at both readings.

act.evidence: Sponsored the Treaty Principles Bill; its 11 MPs were the only votes in favour at the second reading (10 April 2025).

nz-first.evidence: Voted against at the second reading, but its own policy is to remove references to "the principles of the Treaty" from legislation.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Voted against at both readings; MPs led the haka protest at the first reading.

statements.text: The Waitangi Tribunal should be abolished or replaced once historical claims are settled.
statements.explainer: The Waitangi Tribunal (1975) investigates Crown breaches of the Treaty and makes mostly non-binding recommendations.

green.evidence: Implement Waitangi Tribunal recommendations; uphold te Tiriti across government decision-making.

act.evidence: Abolish the Waitangi Tribunal once historical claims are resolved.

nz-first.evidence: Replace the Waitangi Tribunal with a Treaty of Waitangi Completion Commission.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Make Waitangi Tribunal recommendations binding.

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: Increase and entrench Waitangi Tribunal funding and extend its binding jurisdiction on the Crown.

statements.text: The Māori electorates should be abolished, or their future put to a referendum.
statements.explainer: Seven Māori electorates are elected by voters on the Māori roll. Abolishing or entrenching them is a recurring debate.

green.evidence: Entrench the Māori electoral seats.

nz-first.evidence: Introduce a binding referendum on the Māori seats.

statements.text: Government services should be allocated by need alone, without Māori- or ethnicity-specific programmes.
statements.explainer: Since 2023 the government has removed some ethnicity-based targeting (e.g. disestablishing Te Aka Whai Ora, the Māori Health Authority).

labour.evidence: Introduce a Māori-led job training programme and fund; allocate 5% of government procurement to Māori businesses.

green.evidence: Simplify funding for Hauora Māori providers; create a Māori Education Authority.

act.evidence: Remove ethnicity-based criteria for delivering public services.

nz-first.evidence: Disestablish the Independent Māori Statutory Board from Auckland Council; policy is to remove "principles of the Treaty" references from environmental laws.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Invest in Māori health outcomes; Māori-led health, education, disability and justice systems.

nz-loyal.evidence: "Scrap all race-based policies" (party website as quoted by RNZ).

alliance.evidence: Māori health providers keep the option to remain independent with full funding; constitutional change with Te Tiriti at the centre.

conservative.evidence: "Employment, promotion and access to public services should be based on individual need, ability and merit."

vision-nz.evidence: "Completely remove all race-based targeted policies and spending within the healthcare sector"; "End all race-based politics."

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: "Te Aka Motuhake" — an autonomous, state-funded, iwi-governed Māori health authority.

statements.text: The Regulatory Standards Act 2025 should be repealed.
statements.explainer: ACT's Regulatory Standards Act sets "principles of responsible regulation" that new laws are checked against. It passed 68–55 in November 2025.

national.evidence: Voted for the Bill at all three readings; did not answer Greenpeace's repeal question.

labour.evidence: Lodged a member's bill to repeal it (Nov 2025); "Yes" to repealing it in the Greenpeace survey.

green.evidence: "Yes" to repealing the Regulatory Standards Act (Greenpeace survey).

act.evidence: Wrote and sponsored the Act (David Seymour, Minister for Regulation).

nz-first.evidence: Mixed: voted for it in 2025, Winston Peters then said NZ First would repeal it, but its 2026 Greenpeace survey answer did not commit to repeal.

te-pati-maori.evidence: "Yes" to repealing the Regulatory Standards Act (Greenpeace survey).

opportunity.evidence: "Yes" to repealing the Regulatory Standards Act (Greenpeace survey).

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: "As a matter of priority, vote to repeal both the Regulatory Standards Act 2025 and the Treaty Clauses Review."

statements.text: Political donations should be capped, with only New Zealand voters allowed to donate.
statements.explainer: There is no cap on how much a person can donate to a party; companies, trusts and unions can donate.

labour.evidence: No commitment: "Labour believes in transparent and fair rules for political party donations" (Greenpeace survey).

green.evidence: "Yes"; also "capping a donor's donations at a level that does not risk donor influence over policy."

nz-first.evidence: Supports "electoral integrity and transparency" but has no policy restricting donations to voters (Greenpeace survey).

te-pati-maori.evidence: "Yes" to limiting donations to registered voters (Greenpeace survey).

opportunity.evidence: Cap donations at $30,000 per donor per election and ban donations from companies and trusts.

animal-justice.evidence: Committed to "getting money out of politics" (no specific cap stated).

statements.text: Central government should cap how much councils can raise rates each year.
statements.explainer: National proposes keeping annual rates rises within 2–4%; councils argue they need more funding tools for infrastructure.

national.evidence: Instruct councils to keep annual rate increases between 2 and 4 percent.

labour.evidence: Mixed: Barbara Edmonds said Labour supported the rates-cap bill to its first reading, while Tangi Utikere said in Dec 2025 "we don't support this rates cap" (both as quoted by National).

green.evidence: Reject the proposed rates cap and allow councils to use more funding tools.

opportunity.evidence: Give councils more tools to invest in infrastructure (rather than limiting revenue).

statements.text: Overall immigration to New Zealand should be reduced.
statements.explainer: Net migration hit records in 2023 and then fell sharply as more New Zealanders left for Australia.

green.evidence: Increase the refugee quota and support migrant workers to residency.

nz-first.evidence: Replace the Accredited Employer Work Visa with a shortage-led skilled visa; remove automatic student-visa work rights; tie immigration to genuine labour shortages.

conservative.evidence: Cap net immigration of unskilled and semi-skilled workers (zero if social goods are not increasing), while welcoming skilled migrants.

vision-nz.evidence: "Pause mass immigration immediately to review visa policies and relieve pressure on local infrastructure."

statements.text: New residents should have to wait longer (five years or more) before they can get most benefits.
statements.explainer: Most benefits currently need two years' residence. National proposes five; NZ First ten.

national.evidence: Change entitlements for benefits for new NZ residents to five years.

act.evidence: "ACT will introduce a five-year welfare stand-down for residence class visa holders" (2026 Fiscal Plan).

nz-first.evidence: A benefit stand-down period of ten years for migrants, and longer residency for citizenship.

statements.text: The age of eligibility for NZ Superannuation should stay at 65.
statements.explainer: NZ Super is paid to everyone 65+ regardless of income. ACT proposes 67 by 2035; National supports raising it eventually but its 2026 policy is cross-party talks.

national.evidence: Would "have liked to make change" and has long backed 67 from a future date, but its 2026 election policy is only to hold cross-party accord talks on the retirement system.

labour.evidence: "Labour has been clear that it will not means test New Zealand superannuation or increase the age of eligibility."

green.evidence: "Yes. We will retain NZ Superannuation as a universal entitlement from age 65."

act.evidence: Raise the retirement age to 67 by 2035 (three months a year).

nz-first.evidence: "New Zealand First will not support changes to the entitlement or eligibility of New Zealand Superannuation."

te-pati-maori.evidence: Says the age of eligibility "should not be raised at all" and should be lower for Māori because of lower life expectancy (May 2023 statement; no newer position found).

opportunity.evidence: Answered "Yes" to retaining the eligibility age at 65 (Grey Power survey).

alliance.evidence: "Keeps the age of entitlement for Super at 65."

statements.text: Main benefits should be substantially increased.
statements.explainer: Benefits were indexed to wages from 2023, then changed back to inflation indexation by the current government.

national.evidence: Reduce benefit payments for people receiving support for more than two years.

green.evidence: Increase benefit payments and improve standards for beneficiaries.

act.evidence: ACT's 2026 Fiscal Plan has no benefit increases; it tightens eligibility (independent medical certification for health and disability benefits, a five-year stand-down for new residents).

te-pati-maori.evidence: "We will scrap benefit sanctions and ensure everybody is paid enough to live with dignity, whether they are in employment or not" (Oct 2024 press release).

opportunity.evidence: A universal Citizens' Income of up to $370 a week, replacing many main benefits.

alliance.evidence: Proposes a Universal Benefit, individual entitlements, universal child payments and an end to benefit sanctions.

womens-rights.evidence: "Minimum wages and benefits need to be increased so that all people have living incomes."

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: Replace the "complex, punitive benefit system" with a non-taxable Universal Whānau Allowance and wipe MSD/IRD debt for low-income whānau.

statements.text: Beneficiaries should face tougher obligations and sanctions, such as drug tests or payment cuts.
statements.explainer: The government introduced a traffic-light sanctions system in 2025. National proposes drug testing and cuts after two years on a benefit.

national.evidence: Introduce drug testing for people receiving benefits; reduce payments after two years on a benefit; longer stand-downs.

green.evidence: Increase benefit payments and improve standards for beneficiaries; refuse to use AI for welfare decisions.

act.evidence: Restrict medical certification for health-related benefits and monitor spending of long-term jobseekers.

te-pati-maori.evidence: "We will scrap benefit sanctions"; called the traffic-light sanctions system "a tool designed to punish whānau" (Oct 2024 press release).

opportunity.evidence: Citizen's Income replaces most main benefits: "no Work and Income appointments, no relationship status checks—just a guaranteed payment".

alliance.evidence: "An end to benefit sanctions."

conservative.evidence: "Welfare: Reform is needed. Fifty years of expanding welfare has undermined our families and created an underclass."

vision-nz.evidence: "Dismantle state dependency"; "Slash state dependency by eliminating financial rules that disincentivise marriage."

te-tai-tokerau-party.evidence: Replace the "punitive benefit system" and end "relationship status" policing.

statements.text: Transport money should go mainly to public transport and rail rather than new highways.
statements.explainer: The government's priority is "Roads of National Significance"; others favour rapid transit, rail and cheaper fares.

national.evidence: Complete construction of the next set of Roads of National Significance; fund the $800m Christchurch Northern Motorway extension.

labour.evidence: Introduce a $20 weekly public-transport fare cap in the main cities ($10 elsewhere).

green.evidence: Build mass rapid transit in three major cities and invest in better rail and bus links; free or $2 fares.

act.evidence: Focus the National Land Transport Fund on road infrastructure only.

nz-first.evidence: Establish a 12-month trial of commuter rail in Canterbury and further south.

opportunity.evidence: Make public transport free.

alliance.evidence: Publicly owned rail and coastal shipping as "twin backbones" of freight, more public-transport funding.

statements.text: Rules limiting farm pollution of rivers (such as nitrogen limits) should be strengthened rather than loosened.
statements.explainer: The government has loosened some freshwater rules (e.g. Te Mana o te Wai, intensification limits) and is rewriting the RMA.

national.evidence: Supported blocking regional freshwater plans and let restrictions on intensification lapse (Greenpeace assessment).

labour.evidence: Says "freshwater limits should be national bottom lines" and wants councils able to implement the 2020 freshwater policy, but would not commit to lowering the nitrogen cap.

green.evidence: Impose nitrogen caps on all agricultural practices; phase out synthetic nitrogen fertiliser.

act.evidence: Replace Te Mana o te Wai with measurable freshwater outcomes.

nz-first.evidence: "No. Our approach is for practical, science-based freshwater management that balances environmental outcomes with productive land use."

te-pati-maori.evidence: Answered "Yes" to immediately lowering the synthetic nitrogen fertiliser cap and banning new dairy conversions (Greenpeace survey).

opportunity.evidence: Tighten rules on water quality and reinstate Te Mana o te Wai, but did not back a lower fertiliser cap.

animal-justice.evidence: Links intensive dairying to "degradation of waterways"; seeks to transition away from animal agriculture.

statements.text: Rules on gene technology (genetic modification) should be relaxed.
statements.explainer: The Gene Technology Bill would end the effective ban on GM outside the lab; it stalled in 2025–26 after NZ First withheld support.

national.evidence: The Gene Technology Bill is a National-led government bill; National remains in favour (it lacks NZ First's votes to pass).

labour.evidence: Withheld support at select committee citing limited consultation and lack of regulatory independence.

green.evidence: Called the Bill a "radical liberalisation and deregulation of GM technology" and withheld support.

act.evidence: Supports the Gene Technology Bill (with objections to its Māori advisory committee).

nz-first.evidence: Would not support the Bill into law without major changes, calling it "far too liberal" and lacking safeguards.

te-pati-maori.evidence: Told RNZ it "remained opposed to the bill".

opportunity.evidence: Rewrite gene technology regulations to enable modern gene technologies.

conservative.evidence: "We oppose the current government's move to end the long-standing restrictions placed on field trials and the release of genetically modified organisms."

statements.text: New Zealand should formally recognise the State of Palestine now.
statements.explainer: In September 2025 the government decided not to recognise Palestine "yet", unlike the UK, Canada and Australia.

national.evidence: Government (PM Luxon, Foreign Minister Peters) decided in Sept 2025 not to recognise Palestine "yet", calling recognition inevitable but premature while Hamas remains.

labour.evidence: "Labour will recognise the State of Palestine" and place economic sanctions on Israel.

green.evidence: Recognise Palestine as a state and sanction Israel.

nz-first.evidence: Winston Peters announced at the UN in Sept 2025: "we do not think that time is now."

alliance.evidence: "We must demand self-determination for Palestinians and the right to return to their homeland."

free-palestine.evidence: Party exists to press NZ to "uphold its obligations under international law with respect to Palestine"; seeks a single democratic state.

statements.text: Defence spending should rise substantially, towards 2% of GDP.
statements.explainer: The 2025 Defence Capability Plan aims to lift defence spending from about 1% to 2% of GDP by the early 2030s.

national.evidence: National-led government's Defence Capability Plan targets 2% of GDP by 2032/33; Defence Minister Chris Penk reaffirmed "a smooth and steady upward trajectory to 2 percent" in May 2026.

green.evidence: Security policy prioritises peacekeeping and "prevention over military force" and would withdraw NZ from the Five Eyes network; no increase in military spending proposed.

act.evidence: ACT's 2026 Fiscal Plan cuts non-frontline spending but protects "the spending growth since 2017 in core frontline services such as health, education, defence" (no specific 2% target found in its 2026 documents).

te-pati-maori.evidence: Declare NZ a "military neutral" country and focus the Defence Force on protection, disaster response and the Pacific.

alliance.evidence: A "peace-focused defence force", non-alignment and an end to intelligence sharing with the US.

free-palestine.evidence: NZ should withdraw "from any formal security alliances with the U.S." and distance itself from "military interventionism".

statements.text: New Zealand should increase its overseas aid budget.
statements.explainer: NZ spends about 0.25–0.3% of national income on aid; the UN target is 0.7%.

labour.evidence: Increase foreign aid to 0.7 percent of GDP.

green.evidence: Increase climate aid funding to the Pacific.

act.evidence: Reduce NZ's foreign aid to 2017 levels.

alliance.evidence: Developed nations should cancel Global South debts "as a form of reparation".

statements.text: Cannabis should be legalised or decriminalised for personal use.
statements.explainer: A 2020 referendum on legal cannabis narrowly failed (48.4% yes). Medicinal cannabis is legal on prescription.

green.evidence: Decriminalise cannabis for personal use; long-term policy is a legal, regulated cannabis market.

opportunity.evidence: Decriminalise drug possession (but not supply).

nz-outdoors-freedom.evidence: "We do not believe cultivation or possession of cannabis for personal use should be a criminal offense."

legalise-cannabis.evidence: "That the possession, cultivation and use of pure cannabis... be free from prosecution" and a regulated R18 cannabis market.

statements.text: Children under 16 should be banned from social media.
statements.explainer: National's Online Safety bill would make platforms take reasonable steps to keep under-16s off; ACT and NZ First oppose it.

national.evidence: Ban under-16 year olds from social media (Online Safety (Minimum Age...) Bill).

labour.evidence: Backed the bill to pass its first reading and go to select committee, wanting it "substantially improved".

act.evidence: Will vote against: "The ban they propose won't work, and the side effects will leave us worse off" (David Seymour).

nz-first.evidence: Winston Peters said NZ First would "never support this", citing a slippery slope.

opportunity.evidence: Support the online safety bill on an under-16 ban going to select committee.

statements.text: Puberty blockers and other medical gender-transition treatments should not be available to under-18s.
statements.explainer: In December 2025 the government stopped new prescriptions of puberty blockers for gender dysphoria, following the UK.

national.evidence: Health Minister Simeon Brown halted new puberty-blocker prescriptions for gender dysphoria from 19 Dec 2025 as a "precautionary approach".

green.evidence: Free access to gender-affirming health care "including reversal of the ban on puberty blockers".

nz-first.evidence: Campaigned for the ban and announced it ahead of the Ministry; Peters: "we never stopped fighting to make this happen."

conservative.evidence: Restrict irreversible procedures to alter a child's sex characteristics "where there is no clear medical necessity" and require independent assessment.

womens-rights.evidence: Supports the puberty-blocker ban and would extend it to cross-sex hormones for under-18s and surgery for under-25s.

vision-nz.evidence: "Prohibit all medical interventions for gender transition in minors."

statements.text: Abortion law should be made more restrictive.
statements.explainer: Abortion was decriminalised in 2020 (conscience vote). Most parties treat it as a conscience issue and have no party position.

conservative.evidence: Introduce an Unborn Child (Legal Personhood and Rights) Act recognising an unborn child as a legal person from the third trimester (28 weeks).

womens-rights.evidence: Lists "the right to have control of our own bodies, including reproductive autonomy" among the rights it exists to protect.

vision-nz.evidence: Healthcare policy commits to "protecting the sanctity of human life" (no specific abortion law change stated).

electorates.name: Auckland Central
electorates.description: Auckland Central covers Auckland’s city centre, suburbs such as Ponsonby, Newton and Arch Hill, as well as the islands of the Hauraki Gulf. It is currently held by Green party co-leader Chlöe Swabrick, who won the electorate with a margin of 16,624 votes and has held the seat since 2020. National won the party vote in 2023 with 33%, followed by the Green Party on 24%. Barring one three year gap, the seat was held continuously by Labour from 1919-2008, but it has not regained it since.

Since 2020, it has been held by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, who easily won re-election with a margin of 24,769 votes. National also won a majority of the party vote at 58%, more than double second-placed Labour’s 22%. electorates.description: Christchurch Central covers much of inner Christchurch as well as bits from adjoining suburbs such as Sydenham, Beckenham, and Richmond. The electorate has been held by Labour’s Duncan Webb since 2017, who won re-election with 15,553 votes in 2023. National won the party vote in 2023 with 31%, followed by Labour at 28%. In 2011, preliminary results saw a tie on election night, with special votes eventually giving the electorate to National for the first time in its history by just 2 votes.

electorates.name: Coromandel
electorates.description: Coromandel covers the Coromandel peninsula, the Hauraki district, and some of the Bay of Plenty, finishing at the edge of Tauranga. The seat is held by National’s Sam Uffindell, who was first elected in a 2022 by-election, and was re-elected in 2023 with a margin of 18,980. National won the party vote in 2023 with 46%, followed by Labour on 18%. Between 1984 and 2002, the seat was held by current New Zealand First leader Winston Peters, first as a National MP before founding New Zealand First in 1993.

The seat is held by National’s Catherine Wedd, who was first elected in 2023 with a margin of 21,981. National won the party vote in 2023 with 41%, followed by Labour with 25%. The electorate has the highest proportion of labourers in the country, with 22% of the populace employed as labourers, compared to 11% nationally.

National won the party vote in 2023 with 50%, followed by Labour on 18%. The seat boasted the odd distinction of being the birthplace of both 2020 Labour and National leaders Jacinda Ardern and Judith Collins, though neither ran in the electorate.

Waimakariri is the home-ownership capital of New Zealand, with 54% of residents owning their own home, compared to 41% nationally.

The electorate has been reformed for 2026. The seat is held by retiring National MP Paulo Garcia, who is not running again in Waitākere in 2026. Labour won the party vote in Kelston in 2023 with 37%, followed by National on 31%. This is Waitākere’s fourth spell of existence, having previously existed between 1946-66, 1978-87, and 1993-2014.

Green Party MP Tamatha Paul won the former Wellington Central electorate with a margin of 6,066 votes in 2023. She is competing against Labour’s health spokesperson Ayesha Verrall.

The seat is held by National’s Maureen Pugh, a list MP who became an electorate MP in the 2023 election, but is retiring in 2026. Pugh was elected with a margin of 13,317 in 2023. National won the party vote in 2023 with 33% of the vote, followed by Labour with 24%. Geographically, it is the largest general 
electorate in the country.

1law4all.name: 1Law4All Party
1law4all.intro:
Registered for the 2014 election, it failed to lodge a candidate list after four of five board members resigned
shortly before nominations closed. It had earlier removed references to Allan Titford from its website after his
conviction for rape and arson. As an unregistered group it distributed pamphlets in 2017 and 2019; the Advertising
Standards Authority ordered it to stop the 2019 material as likely to cause "serious offence". [1]

act.name: ACT New Zealand
act.intro: The campaign was launched at Shed 10, Auckland, on 28 June 2026 under the theme **"Lock Labour Out, Unlock New Zealand's Potential"**. Seymour named three focuses: government waste, cutting business restrictions, and equal rights under the law ([Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/29-06-2026/aura-edits-and-protests-field-notes-from-the-act-partys-big-flash-rally), [speech on Scoop](https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA2606/S00205.htm)). Broadcaster Paul Henry is fourth on the list. Headline promises, all sourced in [`act.json`](../../data/promises/act.json) and [policies](./policies/README.md):

advance-nz.name: Advance NZ
advance-nz.intro:
Jami-Lee Ross, MP for Botany, left National in 2018 after accusing leader Simon Bridges of corruption over a
$100,000 donation; he was later himself charged by the Serious Fraud Office over the donation scheme and was acquitted
at a High Court trial that began in July 2022, while three co-defendants were convicted. In July 2020 Advance merged campaigns with Billy Te Kahika's NZ Public
Party, a party known for spreading COVID-19 "plandemic" misinformation; other component parties were the NZ People's
Party, Reset NZ and Direct Democracy NZ. [1][2]

alliance.name: Alliance
alliance.intro:
The Alliance was Jim Anderton's left-wing grouping that won 18% of the vote (but only two seats under first-past-the-post)
in 1993, won about 8% and ten seats in 1999 and entered coalition with Labour, introducing paid parental leave and
Kiwibank. It split in 2002 when Anderton's faction left (the Progressives), and
the rump lost all its seats. [1]

animal-justice.name: Animal Justice Party
animal-justice.intro:
The party's 2023 platform included banning recreational fishing and hunting competitions, rodeo, horse racing, fur and
leather production and animal experimentation; supporting the greyhound-racing ban; ending intensive winter grazing
("mud farming") and factory farming; opposing 1080; a commissioner for animals; and a phased shift from animal farming
to plant-based agriculture with support for farmers. It also campaigns against the coalition government's plan to
reverse the 2023 live-export ban. [1]

balance-new-zealand.name: Balance New Zealand

ban-1080.name: Ban 1080 Party
ban-1080.intro:
The party wanted the Department of Conservation's aerial 1080 programme stopped immediately and replaced with
species-specific protection plans and targeted pest control. Its best candidate result was Pete Salter's 6.5% (fourth)
in West Coast-Tasman in 2014. Police visited party officials in 2015 during the investigation into threats to
contaminate infant formula with 1080; the threats were found to be unrelated to the party. After the 2017 result it
deregistered, and many supporters moved to the [Outdoors Party](../nz-outdoors-freedom/README.md). [1][2]

build-the-nation.name: Build the Nation
build-the-nation.intro: A single-candidate label in 2026 (Wikipedia lists Richard McIntosh under 'Build the Nation'; policy.nz lists him as an independent).

civilian.name: The Civilian Party
civilian.intro:
The party drew criticism in 2014 for receiving $33,635 of broadcasting funding; John Key quipped "the biggest joke's
on us, the taxpayer". Uffindell replied that other "joke parties" were getting funding too. It won 1,096 votes (0.05%)
in 2014 and stood no electorate candidates. [1][2]

conservative.name: Conservative Party
conservative.intro:
Businessman Colin Craig, who had organised a 2009 protest march and polled third (8.7%) in the 2010 Auckland mayoralty,
launched the party on 3 August 2011. It absorbed members of the Kiwi Party (Larry Baldock) and New Citizen Party,
spent NZ$1.88 million in 2011 — the second-highest of any party, mostly Craig's own money — and campaigned on raising
the drinking age to 21, parental notification for abortion, repealing the "anti-smacking" law and opposing asset
sales. It won **2.65%**; Craig came second in Rodney. [1]

democracynz.name: DemocracyNZ
democracynz.intro:
King, Northland MP 2017–2020, joined the 2022 anti-mandate protest and left National. In June 2023 five candidates
quit over the party's culture, and many supporters moved to NZ First. DemocracyNZ ran 13 candidates in 2023 and won
**0.24%** (6,786); King came fourth in Northland (3,812 votes). [1][2]

focus-nz.name: Focus New Zealand (Focus NZ, formerly NZ Rural)
focus-nz.intro:
A Northland-based party that stood in the 2013 Far North and Whangārei local elections and the 2014 general election,
where its 639 party votes were the fewest of the 15 registered parties. [1]

free-palestine.name: Free Palestine
free-palestine.intro:
The party was set up in May 2026 to put Gaza and the Palestinian cause at the centre of the 2026 election. On 7 May the
Electoral Commission allocated it $78,887 of broadcasting funding (amended to $82,011), contingent on registration; it
applied in June and was registered on 5 August 2026, but its proposed logo was declined. [1][2]

freedoms-nz.name: Freedoms NZ
freedoms-nz.intro:
Tamaki forecast 20% of the vote. National, Labour, the Greens and ACT all ruled out working with it (National after
initially telling reporters to "read between the lines"). The High Court rejected its challenge to the Electoral
Commission's decision to give the group a single broadcasting allocation. During the 2023 campaign Freedoms NZ supporters,
notably Vision candidate Karl Mokaraka, disrupted Labour, National and ACT events, including Labour's campaign launch.
It won **0.34%** (9,586). [1]

green.name: Green Party
green.intro: The Greens are New Zealand's third-largest party. They have passed the 5% threshold at every election since leaving the Alliance in 1997. Their weakest result was 5.3% in 2005 and their best was 11.6% in 2023. They have helped form three Labour-led governments. Under MMP they have never joined, or given confidence and supply to, a National-led government. The Greens hold four values: ecological wisdom, social justice, grassroots democracy and non-violence. They also accept Te Tiriti o Waitangi as the country's founding document.

heartland.name: Heartland New Zealand Party (HeartlandNZ)
heartland.intro:
Backed at its founding by Hamilton entrepreneur Harry Mowbray, Heartland ran a five-person list in 2020 and won 914
party votes (0.03%), the fewest of any registered party, though Ball polled 8,462 electorate votes (21%, third) in Port
Waikato. [1][2]

independent-taranaki.name: Independent Taranaki
independent-taranaki.intro: A single-candidate label in 2026 (policy.nz lists the candidate as an independent).

internet-party.name: Internet Party
internet-party.intro:
Kim Dotcom — the Megaupload founder whose Auckland home was raided in January 2012 at the request of US authorities —
announced the Internet Party in January 2014. It signed up members through a phone app and was registered on 13 May
2014. Dotcom gave it NZ$3.5 million, described as the largest personal contribution to a New Zealand party on record.
Former Alliance MP and minister Laila Harré was chosen as leader. [1]

jobseeker-party.name: Jobseeker Party

labour.name: Labour Party
labour.intro: Labour's 1916 objective was "the socialisation of the means of production, distribution and exchange"; the socialist objective was dropped in 1951. The current constitution lists democratic-socialist principles — management of natural resources for all, equal access regardless of wealth, co-operation in economic relations "to ensure a just distribution of wealth", the right to work, people "more important than property", **honouring Te Tiriti o Waitangi**, international co-operation, and equality regardless of race, sex, sexuality, gender identity, age, religion or disability. Observers describe its policy as pragmatic social democracy with social-liberal positions ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Labour_Party)).

legalise-cannabis.name: Aotearoa Legalise Cannabis
legalise-cannabis.intro:
The ALCP has contested every general election since 1996 and many by-elections without winning a seat. Its best
results were 1.66% (1996) and 1.10% (1999); since then it has stayed below 1%. Former ALCP candidates Nándor Tánczos and
Metiria Turei later became Green MPs (Turei was Green co-leader), and Tim Shadbolt became Invercargill's mayor. Former
deputy leader Abe Gray later joined TOP. [1]

leighton-baker.name: Leighton Baker Party
leighton-baker.intro:
Baker, arrested during the 2022 Wellington protest, launched the party after being replaced as New Conservative
leader. It won **0.07%** (2,105) in 2023; Baker came fourth in Waimakariri (3.9%). He said: "maybe there's not that
many people that agree with us, but we still have an obligation to present a different view." After the election the
Electoral Commission admitted data-entry errors at three booths had wrongly assigned hundreds of votes to the Leighton
Baker Party and New Conservatives (corrected; seat allocation unaffected). See also [Conservative](../conservative/README.md). [1][2][3]

libertarianz.name: Libertarianz
libertarianz.intro:
Libertarianz contested every election from 1996 (best: 0.29% in 1999). In 2006 member Bernard Darnton sued Helen
Clark over Labour's publicly funded 2005 pledge card. Its last general election was 2011 (0.07%). In January 2014 leader
Richard McGrath asked the Electoral Commission to deregister it, saying volunteer administration had become impossible,
and advised members to support ACT under its new president Jamie Whyte. [1]

mana.name: Mana Movement
mana.intro: Party-vote figures: official results as tabulated by Wikipedia (`raw/minor-parties/results.json`). [4]

money-free-party.name: Money Free Party NZ
money-free-party.intro: Part of the international Money Free movement, which advocates a resource-based economy in which all work is voluntary (inspired by Jacque Fresco's Venus Project). Never registered: it could not verify 500 members for 2014. Results: five electorate candidates in 2014; four in 2017 (293 votes in total); two in 2020 and two in 2023. Osmaston is a frequent mayoral candidate.

nap.name: Not A Party (NAP)
nap.intro: An unregistered 'anti-voting' group (Wikipedia lists its ideology as anti-voting; its website includes posts such as 'Democracy is the worst form of government'). Candidate Richard Goode contested Mana in 2023.

national.name: National Party
national.intro: National is New Zealand's main centre-right party. It is the senior partner in the current coalition government with ACT and NZ First, and it has led a government six times since 1936, more often than any other party. Its 2026 slogan is **"Fixing the Basics. Building the Future."**

new-nation.name: New Nation Party
new-nation.intro:
A founding component of Freedoms NZ, it left in July 2023 to stand on its own and won 1,530 votes (0.05%) — the
lowest of any party in 2023. Its candidate in the 2022 Tauranga by-election, former councillor Andrew Hollis, won 260
votes. [1][2]

new-world-order-mccann-party.name: New World Order McCann Party
new-world-order-mccann-party.intro: A single-candidate label in 2026; Wikipedia links it to the long-running joke 'New World Order Party' label.

newzeal.name: NewZeal
newzeal.intro:
ONE Party launched at Marsden Cross in June 2020, made a reciprocal electorate arrangement with Vision NZ and won
0.28% (8,121). In 2022 it jointly backed a New Conservative candidate in the Hamilton West by-election. Former National
minister **Alfred Ngaro** — who said he was disappointed by National's stance on conversion therapy and gender identity —
took over and renamed it NewZeal in 2023; it won 0.57% (16,126). On 22 March 2026 Ngaro announced at Winston Peters'
State of the Nation speech that he would stand for NZ First, citing "strategic realism and shared values", and the party
deregistered. [1][2]

nz-economic-euthenics-party.name: (NZ) Economic Euthenics
nz-economic-euthenics-party.intro: The label used by perennial Christchurch candidate Tubby Hansen, who contested Wigram in 2023.

nz-independent-coalition.name: NZ Independent Coalition
nz-independent-coalition.intro:
Brendan Horan was expelled from NZ First in December 2012 amid accusations (which he denied) of taking money from his
dying mother's bank account. He formed the party for the 2014 election on the slogan "safe children, safe whanau, safe
society". It won 872 votes (0.04%) and Horan left Parliament. [1][2]

nz-loyal.name: NZ Loyal
nz-loyal.intro:
The party won **1.21%** (34,478 votes) and none of its 33 electorate candidates won. Because it missed the nomination
deadline for most of its intended 15-person list, its official list held only three names (one of whom left the party);
the High Court refused to let it add names after the deadline ("If you leave it to the last minute and something goes
wrong, the responsibility falls squarely on the party"). Had it passed 5%, most of its seats would have been left
empty. [1]

nz-outdoors-freedom.name: NZ Outdoors & Freedom
nz-outdoors-freedom.intro:
The Outdoors Party stood four candidates in 2017 (0.06%). After the Ban 1080 Party deregistered, many of its
supporters joined, and anti-1080 lawyer **Sue Grey** became co-leader around the start of 2020. During 2020 it called the
COVID-19 lockdown "cruel and unreasonable" and compared the government to the Nazi Party; an Auckland rally in June 2020
featured 9/11 "false flag", flat-earth and anti-5G claims and the harassment of a young Asian woman (Grey said those
involved were not party members). Several candidates defected before the 2020 election (0.11%). [1]

nz-peoples-party.name: New Zealand People's Party (2015–2019)
nz-peoples-party.intro:
Nauhria came third (4.2%) in the 2016 Mount Roskill by-election; Winston Peters called the party a "National Party
front". It won 1,890 votes (0.07%) in 2017 with six list candidates and joined Advance NZ in 2020. For the 2026
"People's Party New Zealand" electorate candidates see [peoples-party-new-zealand](../peoples-party-new-zealand/README.md)
— our sources do not establish a connection. [1]

nz-tea-party.name: New Zealand TEA Party (Taxpayers and Entrepreneurs Alliance)
nz-tea-party.intro:
Unconnected to the US Tea Party. Candidate John Palino campaigned for an electorate from Florida. It won 2,414 votes
(0.08%) in 2020. [1][2]

opportunity.name: The Opportunity Party (TOP)
opportunity.intro: Source: official results as tabulated by Wikipedia (`raw/minor-parties/results.json`). [13]

peoples-party-new-zealand.name: People's Party New Zealand
peoples-party-new-zealand.intro: Two electorate candidates in South Auckland seats. A 'People's Party NZ Inc.' was originally allocated $78,887 of broadcasting money by the Electoral Commission on 7 May 2026, but its amended allocation was $0 because it did not become a registered party. Our sources do not establish whether it is connected to the earlier New Zealand People's Party (2015–19, see ../nz-peoples-party/).

pirate-party.name: Pirate Party of New Zealand
pirate-party.intro:
As an unregistered party it could not contest the party vote. In 2011 it stood in the Botany by-election (32 votes)
and in Hamilton East (137 votes) and Wellington Central (277 votes) at the general election, after being conditionally
awarded $20,000 of broadcasting funding and having its logo registered. It stood no candidates in 2014 and failed to
gain registration for 2017. [1]

progressive-aotearoa-new-zealand.name: Progressive Party of Aotearoa New Zealand (Progressive Aotearoa, PPANZ)
progressive-aotearoa-new-zealand.intro: An unregistered party based on Prabhat Ranjan Sarkar's Progressive Utilization Theory (economic democracy; turning large businesses into co-operatives). It stood two electorate candidates in 2020 (Dyer won 50 votes in Nelson) and Dyer alone in 2023. In August 2026 it announced three candidates. Not to be confused with Jim Anderton's former Progressive Party.

social-credit.name: Social Credit (Democrats for Social Credit / New Zealand Democratic Party for Social Credit)
social-credit.intro:
New Zealand's third party from the 1950s to the 1980s, Social Credit was part of the Alliance from 1991 to 2002 and
briefly of the Progressive Coalition, then re-established itself as an independent party. In this archive's period it
was a fringe party: 0.08% in 2011, 0.07% in 2014, 0.03% in 2017 and 0.05% under the restored Social Credit name in 2020.
In 2021 it opposed COVID-19 vaccine mandates. After deregistration its president Gloria Bruni said it intended to
rebrand to avoid comparison with China's "social credit system". [1][2]

socialist-equality-group.name: Socialist Equality Group

sustainable-nz.name: Sustainable New Zealand Party (Sustainable NZ)
sustainable-nz.intro:
Former party secretary Helen Cartwright alleged in February 2020 that she had been asked to falsify membership records
to reach the 500 needed for registration; Tava said the party complied fully with the Electoral Act. Cartwright left and
founded the Integrity Party. Sustainable NZ received a $53,840 broadcasting allocation and won 1,880 votes (0.07%) in
2020. [1][2]

te-pati-hira.name: Te Pāti Hira

te-pati-maori.name: Te Pāti Māori
te-pati-maori.intro:
Te Pāti Māori is the only party built entirely around Māori political self-determination. Its career has had three
phases:

te-tai-tokerau-party.name: Te Tai Tokerau Party
te-tai-tokerau-party.intro:
Kapa-Kingi won Te Tai Tokerau for [Te Pāti Māori](../te-pati-maori/README.md) in 2023 (by 517 votes over Labour's Kelvin
Davis). After tensions with the party leadership she was suspended in October 2025 and then expelled by its National
Council. policy.nz records that the suspension followed "accusations of mismanaging funds". On 10 March 2026 the High
Court (Justice Paul Radich) ruled the suspension and expulsion unlawful because the process did not follow the party's
kawa and tikanga as its constitution required. Te Pāti Māori accepted the ruling, but in May 2026 Stuff reported that the
two were not working together. [1][2][3]

united-future.name: United Future
united-future.intro:
United Future was formed for the 2002 election by merging Peter Dunne's liberal United New Zealand (founded by
moderate Labour and National MPs in 1995) with Future New Zealand, a "secularised" successor to the Christian
Democrats. Helped by a strong televised-debate performance by Dunne, it won 6.7% and eight seats in 2002, but fell to
2.7% and three seats in 2005 and, after its socially conservative wing (Gordon Copeland, Larry Baldock and others)
left over the 2007 "anti-smacking" law to form what became the Kiwi Party, to a single seat — Dunne's — from 2008.
Dunne then rebranded the party as a moderate centrist party. [1]

vision-nz.name: Vision NZ
vision-nz.intro:
Vision NZ is the third party linked to the Tamakis' Destiny Church, after Destiny New Zealand (2003–07) and the Family
Party (2007–10). Its positions have included opposition to abortion and homosexuality, a call to ban construction of
new mosques, a (later qualified) two-year halt to immigration and refugees, removing non-citizen permanent residents'
right to vote — alongside support for a Māori-owned bank, Tūhoe ownership of Te Urewera and government funding for
Destiny Church programmes. Labour and National ruled out working with it by December 2019. [1]

womens-rights.name: Women's Rights Party
womens-rights.intro:
Jill Ovens, a trade unionist and former Alliance co-leader, resigned from the Labour Party in 2023 over its support for
transgender rights and founded the Women's Rights Party. policy.nz notes that co-leader Dawn Trenberth, also a trade
unionist, had been a Labour member, and that both "left the Labour Party in 2023, feeling alienated by increased
hostility to trans-critical feminist perspectives". [1][2]

mana.promise: Government-funded breakfast and lunch programmes in all decile 1 and 2 schools ('Feed the Kids' bill)
mana.detail: Hone Harawira's Education (Breakfast and Lunch Programmes in Schools) Amendment Bill was drawn from the member's ballot on 8 November 2012 but did not become law while Mana held its seat; Mana left Parliament in 2014. (Mana was in opposition and could not pass it alone.)

mana.promise: Stop the sale of state-owned energy companies
mana.detail: Outcome not achieved: the National-led government's mixed-ownership sell-downs of Genesis, Meridian and Mighty River Power went ahead. Mana was in opposition.

mana.promise: Internet Party–Mana memorandum: Mana to hold list places 1, 3 and 4 and the parties to review the arrangement within five weeks of the election
mana.detail: List ordered as agreed; after reviews the alliance was dissolved on 13 December 2014.

mana.promise: Memorandum with the Māori Party: Mana not to contest other Māori electorates in exchange for a clear run in Te Tai Tokerau
mana.detail: Mana stood only in Te Tai Tokerau and Māngere; Harawira lost Te Tai Tokerau to Kelvin Davis 12,673 to 7,866.

te-pati-maori.promise: Repeal the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 and restore Māori access to the courts for customary title
te-pati-maori.made: Founding kaupapa (2004); 2008 National–Māori Party confidence and supply agreement
te-pati-maori.detail: The party was founded over this issue. In the 2008 agreement National committed only to review the 2004 Act. The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 replaced it and passed 63–56, supported by National, the Māori Party and United Future. Labour, the Greens, ACT and Hone Harawira voted against. The new Act restored the right to go to court for customary title. Tariana Turia backed it while calling it 'drafted by politics, rather than what is fair and moral'. Harawira quit the party over the compromise and formed Mana. In October 2025 the National-led government's amendment raised the legal test for customary marine title. Te Pāti Māori opposed it, and its MPs burned a copy outside Parliament.

te-pati-maori.promise: Protect (and entrench) the Māori electorates
te-pati-maori.detail: National had campaigned on abolishing the Māori seats. In the 2008 agreement it promised not to remove them 'without the consent of the Māori people', and it kept that promise. The seats still exist in 2026. Entrenchment, the Māori Party's own aim, was shelved: both parties agreed they would 'not be pursuing the entrenchment of the Māori seats this parliamentary term'.

te-pati-maori.promise: A review of constitutional arrangements, including Māori representation
te-pati-maori.detail: The review began in 2011 as a commitment under the agreement. We found no evidence in this pass that it led to significant constitutional change. Te Pāti Māori's 2026 programme (Mātike Mai, a Te Tiriti Commission, a 2040 target) shows the party sees this as unfinished business.

te-pati-maori.promise: Whānau Ora: whānau-centred, Māori-led delivery of health and social services
te-pati-maori.made: 2008 agreement (Turia's flagship); made a cornerstone of the 2011 agreement
te-pati-maori.detail: Announced in April 2010 with Turia as Minister for Whānau Ora. Three commissioning agencies were set up in 2014. It is the party's most lasting policy achievement. Critics, including Winston Peters, said its outcomes were hard to measure and that funding was concentrated in Turia's electorate. In 2025 the National-led government re-tendered the contracts, and the Whānau Ora Commissioning Agency, led by party president John Tamihere, lost its contract. Te Puni Kōkiri also ordered a review into whether Whānau Ora money had been used for 'electioneering', namely an advertising campaign urging Māori to join the Māori roll.

te-pati-maori.promise: New Zealand to support the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP)
te-pati-maori.made: Māori Party policy; secured during the 2008–11 term
te-pati-maori.detail: Pita Sharples, as Māori Affairs Minister, announced New Zealand's support at the UN Permanent Forum on 20 April 2010. Under Labour in 2007, New Zealand had been one of four countries to vote against the declaration. Sharples credited the National–Māori Party relationship. Support was for a 'non-binding' declaration. Making UNDRIP enforceable remains a 2026 Te Pāti Māori goal.

te-pati-maori.promise: Cut smoking (Turia's tobacco agenda): higher tobacco excise, plain packaging, Smokefree 2025
te-pati-maori.detail: In 2011 the government adopted a Smokefree 2025 goal, with steep excise increases and later plain packaging, all led by Turia. A separate Labour smokefree-generation law (2022) was repealed by the National-led government in February 2024, which Te Pāti Māori opposed.

te-pati-maori.promise: A new Māori language law giving Māori a stronger role in revitalising te reo
te-pati-maori.made: 2014 confidence and supply term (Te Ururoa Flavell as Minister for Māori Development)
te-pati-maori.detail: Te Ture mō Te Reo Māori 2016 (the Māori Language Act 2016) set up Te Mātāwai to act for iwi and Māori on language revitalisation. It was enacted in both te reo Māori and English, a first for New Zealand.

te-pati-maori.promise: Reform Māori land law (Te Ture Whenua Māori Bill)
te-pati-maori.detail: Flavell's bill was introduced in 2016. It proved controversial and did not pass before the 2017 election. The new Labour minister withdrew it. Smaller targeted amendments passed in 2020.

te-pati-maori.promise: Recognition of the New Zealand Wars
te-pati-maori.detail: A national day of commemoration for the New Zealand Wars began in 2017 and is held on 28 October. It followed a 2015 petition from Ōtorohanga College students. After the 2017 defeat, Marama Fox credited Flavell with this, with the pardon of Rua Kenana, and with UNDRIP support. The Māori Party was one of several actors involved.

te-pati-maori.promise: Win back the Māori electorates through an electoral pact with Mana (2017)
te-pati-maori.made: February 2017 (the Māori Party stood aside in Te Tai Tokerau for Hone Harawira)
te-pati-maori.detail: Labour won all seven Māori seats in 2017. Flavell lost Waiariki, and the party left Parliament on 1.18% of the party vote. Metro magazine and others put the defeat down to a backlash against nine years of supporting National.

te-pati-maori.promise: An independent Māori Health Authority
te-pati-maori.detail: Te Pāti Māori was not in government, but Labour created Te Aka Whai Ora, a Māori Health Authority, in its 2022 health reforms. The National-led government abolished it under urgency on 28 February 2024. The 2026 platform promises 'investment in Māori health outcomes'.

te-pati-maori.promise: No coalition with the right (National/ACT)
te-pati-maori.detail: This reversed the party's 2008–17 approach of working with National. Te Pāti Māori stayed in opposition after 2023. In 2026 it is asking supporters to give their electorate vote to Te Pāti Māori and their party vote to Labour or the Greens, to remove the coalition.

te-pati-maori.promise: Disclose political donations as the law requires
te-pati-maori.detail: In April 2021 the Electoral Commission referred the party to Police for failing to disclose about $320,000 of donations in time. They included $158,224 from then co-leader John Tamihere and $120,000 from Aotearoa Te Kahu LP. Police passed the case to the Serious Fraud Office, which closed it in 2022 without charges. The party blamed volunteers who did not know the rules. In 2022 Charities Services also examined loans and payments to Tamihere's 2020 campaigns from charities he leads (Te Whānau o Waipareira Trust, NUMA).

te-pati-maori.promise: Stand candidates in general (non-Māori) electorates at the 2026 election
te-pati-maori.detail: By October 2026 the party was standing only seven candidates, one in each Māori electorate. Its party list has one name, party secretary Lance Norman. This fits its strategic-voting call, but it reverses the 2025 announcement.

te-pati-maori.promise: Contest all seven Māori electorates in 2026
te-pati-maori.detail: Candidates are standing in all seven seats, including Aperahama Edwards in Te Tai Tokerau and Lisa Marie Murch in Te Tai Tonga. Those two electorate committees had resigned in support of Kapa-Kingi and Ferris. The party is up against two of its own former MPs: Kapa-Kingi (Te Tai Tokerau Party) and Tākuta Ferris (independent).

te-pati-maori.promise: A Parliamentary Commissioner for Te Tiriti with power to audit and veto non-compliant bills, as a coalition 'bottom line'
te-pati-maori.detail: Labour's Chris Hipkins said he would not support a commissioner able to overturn laws, though he was open to better 'checks and balances'. The 2026 package of 1 September 2026 proposes an independent Te Tiriti Commission to investigate Crown breaches, binding Waitangi Tribunal recommendations, a 2040 constitutional-reform target and a $200m Mātike Mai fund. Labour has ruled out the Commission and Mātike Mai. We found no 2026 source confirming whether the veto power or the 'bottom line' status still stands.

te-pati-maori.promise: Abolish prisons by 2040 in favour of community-led solutions
te-pati-maori.detail: Labour said it was 'dead-set against' the policy.

te-pati-maori.promise: 'Kiwi Tax Plan': a 48% rate on income over $300,000, a rebate for people earning under $30,000, a wealth tax, a higher company tax rate, land-banking and vacant-home taxes, a 5% stamp duty and no GST on kai
te-pati-maori.made: 2026 election (26 August 2026); largely repeats the 2023 tax plan
te-pati-maori.detail: This is very close to the 2023 package (zero tax under $30,000, 48% over $300,000, 33% company tax, a wealth tax, GST off food), which shows consistency over time. None of it was enacted in 2023–26, when the party was in opposition.

te-pati-maori.promise: A $1 billion fund for Māori and community ownership of new renewable energy ('energy sovereignty')
Give Māori collectives Crown-owned land and $100m to set up supermarket chains
A $200m Takatāpui Commission
te-pati-maori.detail: RNZ reported the pledge as '$200 million to change who holds power for decisions about takatāpui' (Māori LGBTQ+ people). Check the exact powers proposed in the party's policy document.

national.promise: Not raise GST ("National is not going to be raising GST" - John Key, 2008 campaign)
national.detail: GST was raised from 12.5% to 15% on 1 October 2010 as part of a 'tax switch' that also cut income tax (top rate 38% -> 33%). Key argued he had been asked about raising GST to cover deficits and that the switch was revenue-neutral overall; Labour and commentators called it a broken promise. Verdict: broken on its plain wording, with the mitigating context that it was paired with income-tax cuts.

national.promise: Keep the NZ Super eligibility age at 65 (Key: would resign rather than raise it)
national.detail: The age stayed at 65 throughout Key's premiership (2008-2016). His successor Bill English explicitly declined to repeat the pledge in December 2016 and in March 2017 announced a plan to lift the age to 67 from 2040 (see 2017 entry). Kept for the terms in which it was made.

national.promise: Extend 90-day employment trial periods (first to small firms, then all employers)
national.detail: Employment Relations Amendment Act 2008 allowed firms with fewer than 20 staff to use 90-day trials; extended to all employers in 2010. (Labour later restricted it; National restored it for all employers in December 2023 - see 2023 entry.)

national.promise: Return the Crown accounts to an operating (OBEGAL) surplus in 2014/15
national.detail: Treasury's audited 2014/15 accounts (released 14 October 2015) showed an OBEGAL surplus of $414 million (0.2% of GDP) - narrowly, and better than the May 2015 Budget forecast of a deficit. Often remembered as missed because forecasts through 2015 showed a deficit, but the final result was a small surplus.
